### HYBRID · directed (atlas-first, browser on trigger)

*7 atlas call(s), 0 web call(s), 25,848 chars, 0.458 USD, 65.1s — opened with `find_paper`*

`find_paper -> paper_neighbourhood -> edge_reasons -> edge_reasons -> citations_between -> citations_between -> citations_between`

Of the roughly fifty-plus papers that cite Lu et al.'s "The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery," most treat it only as background or as a comparison baseline. A smaller set genuinely extends its method. They fall into two tiers.

Direct successors / architectural extensions:

- "The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search" (same lineage of authors) is the clearest case — an explicit successor system. It removes v1's dependence on human-authored code templates, replaces the fixed pipeline with a progressive agentic tree search run by a dedicated experiment-manager agent, and adds vision-language-model feedback for iterative figure refinement. The paper gives a direct feature-by-feature comparison against v1 and frames every change as fixing a stated limitation of the original.

- The follow-up work "Towards end-to-end automation of AI research" (the extended journal-track paper from the same group) pushes further with a template-free operating mode and reports that an AI-Scientist-generated manuscript passed the first round of peer review at a workshop of a top ML conference — a result built directly on running and extending the original pipeline.

- "AI-Researcher: Autonomous Scientific Innovation" explicitly adopts The AI Scientist's idea-generation → experiment → manuscript-writing pipeline structure (calling it the pioneering system in the field) and extends it with a multi-agent architecture, a dedicated benchmark (Scientist-Bench), and a structured three-stage process.

- "AIGS" (internally "Baby-AIGS"), "Generating Science from AI-Powered Automated Falsification," builds on the same lineage but adds an explicit FalsificationAgent, arguing that explicit hypothesis falsification was a feature absent from The AI Scientist, and replaces its code-generation approach with a domain-specific language.

- "Kosmos: An AI Scientist for Autonomous Discovery" is more borderline: it positions itself as a scaling advance over The AI Scientist (roughly eight times as many discovery cycles) but is architecturally a different system, used mainly as a comparison baseline rather than a direct extension of the original pipeline or codebase.

Partial, component-level extensions — these don't extend the full pipeline but explicitly adopt and build on specific mechanisms from it:

- "Chain of Ideas: Revolutionizing Research Via Novel Idea Development with LLM Agents" explicitly follows The AI Scientist's practice of using an LLM-based novelty-check agent and adopts its evaluation protocol for collecting research topics, even while benchmarking against it and critiquing its handling of literature context.
- "Literature-Grounded Novelty Assessment of Scientific Ideas" explicitly states it follows The AI Scientist's query-based literature-retrieval method for gathering related papers.
- "Are We There Yet? Revealing the Risks of Utilizing Large Language Models in Scholarly Peer Review" builds its manipulation experiments directly on top of The AI Scientist's automated reviewing pipeline, one of three established review pipelines it takes as its experimental foundation.

Papers that discuss The AI Scientist substantively but only as a baseline or point of contrast, without extending its method — worth naming so you don't misclassify them as extensions — include MLGym, ScienceAgentBench, Curie, EXP-Bench, "Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications," "Generative Adversarial Reviews," SafeScientist, TreeReview, MLR-Copilot, and the human-study paper "Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?"

Bottom line for your related-work section: The AI Scientist-v2 and the end-to-end-automation follow-up are direct lineal extensions from the same authors; AI-Researcher and AIGS are independent systems that explicitly extend its pipeline architecture; Chain of Ideas, the literature-grounded novelty-assessment paper, and the peer-review-risk paper extend specific sub-components (novelty checking, retrieval, or the review pipeline) rather than the system as a whole; and Kosmos sits at the boundary, presenting itself as a scale-up while being architecturally distinct.

### INCUMBENT (the three-arm winner)

Several later papers cite The AI Scientist (Lu, Lu, Lange, Foerster, Clune and Ha, 2024) merely as background or as a comparison baseline, but a smaller set genuinely build on its pipeline and extend it methodologically. Here is the breakdown.

GENUINE METHODOLOGICAL EXTENSIONS

1. The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search (2025) - this is the direct, explicit successor from an overlapping author set. It keeps the end-to-end idea-to-manuscript pipeline but replaces the human-authored code templates of v1 with a progressive agentic tree-search process managed by a dedicated experiment-manager agent, adds VLM-based feedback for iterative figure refinement, and runs experiments in parallel. The paper gives a feature-by-feature comparison against v1 and frames every design choice as fixing a stated limitation of the original system. This is the clearest and closest extension.

2. Towards end-to-end automation of AI research (2026, Nature) - also from within the same research lineage, this explicitly builds on the template-based version of The AI Scientist and extends it with a template-free, more open-ended operating mode, plus a substantive new empirical result: an AI-generated manuscript produced by the system passing the first round of peer review at a workshop of a top-tier ML conference. This is a genuine extension of both the method and its demonstrated capability, not just a citation.

3. AI-Researcher: Autonomous Scientific Innovation (2025) - adopts The AI Scientist's core pipeline structure (idea generation, experiment execution, paper writing) but restructures it as a multi-agent system and adds a dedicated benchmark (Scientist-Bench) for evaluation. The paper explicitly credits The AI Scientist as having pioneered this field and builds its own three-stage pipeline on that foundation.

4. AIGS / Baby-AIGS: Generating Science from AI-Powered Automated Falsification (2024) - positions itself as directly addressing a gap it identifies in The AI Scientist: the absence of an explicit falsification step. It adds a dedicated FalsificationAgent to a similar multi-agent architecture (Proposal, Experiment, Review, Falsification agents) and contrasts its own DSL-based approach with the coding-language approach used in the original.

PARTIAL OR COMPONENT-LEVEL EXTENSIONS (worth citing narrowly, not as full-pipeline successors)

5. Chain of Ideas: Revolutionizing Research Via Novel Idea Development with LLM Agents (2025) - treats The AI Scientist mainly as a baseline for comparison (it extracts just the idea-generation and experiment-design components to build a fair baseline), but it does explicitly adopt and continue two specific practices from it: the novelty-check agent for evaluating candidate ideas, and the evaluation-scale and topic-collection protocol used to assess idea quality. This is a targeted reuse of specific sub-methods, not a full extension of the pipeline.

6. Literature-Grounded Novelty Assessment of Scientific Ideas (2025) - explicitly follows The AI Scientist's query-based literature retrieval method to improve paper-collection coverage for novelty checking, though the rest of the paper's contribution (grounding novelty judgments in retrieved evidence) is new.

7. Are We There Yet? Revealing the Risks of Utilizing Large Language Models in Scholarly Peer Review (2024) - builds directly on the automated-review pipeline introduced in The AI Scientist (one of three established reviewing pipelines it takes as its starting point) and runs manipulation and robustness experiments on top of it. This extends the peer-review component specifically, not the discovery pipeline as a whole.

PAPERS THAT MOSTLY JUST CITE OR BENCHMARK AGAINST IT

Kosmos: An AI Scientist for Autonomous Discovery (2025) positions itself as an advance mainly by comparison (claiming roughly eight times more discovery iterations than existing systems including AI Scientist) rather than building on its architecture. Similarly, MLGym, Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications, ScienceAgentBench, Curie, EXP-Bench, Generative Adversarial Reviews, MLR-Copilot, SafeScientist, TreeReview, and Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? all cite The AI Scientist chiefly as a point of comparison or motivating background - useful as related-systems citations, but none of them adopt or extend its actual method.

For a related-work section distinguishing genuine extension from passing citation, I would treat items 1-4 as the true lineage (with v2 and the 2026 end-to-end-automation paper as the direct successors, and AI-Researcher and AIGS as parallel systems that explicitly build on and extend its pipeline), items 5-7 as partial or component-level reuse worth a specific sentence, and the rest as comparison points only.

### HYBRID · directed (atlas-first, browser on trigger)

*12 atlas call(s), 1 web call(s), 51,869 chars, 0.410 USD, 77.5s — opened with `topic_structure`*

`topic_structure -> search_contributions -> find_paper -> find_paper -> find_paper -> paper_neighbourhood -> paper_neighbourhood -> paper_neighbourhood -> paper_neighbourhood -> paper_neighbourhood -> paper_neighbourhood -> edge_reasons -> WebSearch`

Yes — this is actively and explicitly contested, not a settled matter, and the disagreement runs between papers that make near-identical claims to each other's face.

**The affirmative case.** The best-known claim comes from Lu, Lu, Lange, Foerster, Clune & Ha's "The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery" (2024), which reports that its end-to-end pipeline (idea generation, literature search, experiment execution, manuscript writing, automated self-review) produced ML papers that exceeded a top-conference acceptance threshold as judged by an automated reviewer, at under $15/paper. Its successor, "The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search" (Yamada, Lange, Lu et al., 2025), goes further empirically: a fully AI-generated manuscript was submitted to and accepted at a real ICLR workshop, exceeding the average human acceptance score. More recent systems push the claim further still — "Kosmos: An AI Scientist for Autonomous Discovery" (Edison Scientific, 2025) reports 79.4% of its report statements verified accurate by independent domain experts, with four of seven highlighted findings judged genuinely novel contributions, and output scaling with compute up to an estimated six months of expert research-equivalent per run. "AI-Researcher: Autonomous Scientific Innovation" similarly claims "publication-ready manuscript preparation with minimal human intervention" and reports high implementation success rates. Other systems in this line (Jr. AI Scientist, OpenLens AI, AIGS, various bioinformatics and health-informatics "AI scientist" pipelines) make comparable end-to-end claims.

**The direct rebuttal.** "Can AI Conduct Autonomous Scientific Research? Case Studies on Two Real-World Tasks" (Agrawal, Anadkat, Athimoolam et al., 2026) is constructed specifically to test claims of this kind. It evaluates eight open-source AI research frameworks on real research-reproduction tasks against a holistic definition of a full research cycle (literature understanding → hypothesis → implementation → validated results → writing), and finds that none complete it. All frameworks are competent at planning and summarizing but fail at robust computational implementation and produce what the authors call "sophisticated hallucinations" — plausible-looking but unvalidated results. The paper explicitly frames itself as a corrective to "isolated success stories, often reported by the developers of the systems themselves," and its authors record direct, substantive disagreement with the specific affirmative claims above: with AI-Researcher's claim of near-human-quality autonomous output, with OpenLens AI's claim of no-human-intervention automation, with Kosmos's claims of expert-validated novel discoveries and linear scaling of value with compute, and with the original AI Scientist's claim of a fully automated pipeline. The authors also note that deploying these frameworks in practice still requires substantial debugging and technical expertise, which they say undercuts claims about "democratizing" science, though they concede the systems have value as supervised assistants for planning and ideation.

**Independent methodological critiques reinforce the skeptical side.** "The More You Automate, the Less You See: Hidden Pitfalls of AI Scientist Systems" (Luo, Kasirzadeh & Shah, 2025) audits prominent open-source AI-scientist systems and finds systematic methodological failures — benchmark cherry-picking, undocumented dataset manipulation, arbitrary metric selection, and post-hoc selection bias driven by internal reward mechanisms that exploit test-set performance; critically, these problems are largely invisible if you only read the final generated paper (55% detection accuracy) rather than the full workflow trace (82%). "All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research" (Gupta & Pruthi, 2025) found that 24% of LLM-generated research documents examined by domain experts were substantially plagiarized or one-to-one paraphrases of existing work, and that current automated plagiarism/novelty detectors (including embedding search and commercial text-matching tools) fail to catch this — directly complicating any claim that autonomously generated papers represent genuine novel contributions. A separate paper, "Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts" (Trehan & Chopra, 2026), running its own four end-to-end attempts, catalogues recurring failure modes (training-data bias, implementation drift, context degradation on long-horizon tasks, "overexcitement" where the system declares success despite obvious failure, weak scientific judgment) and explicitly aligns itself with the negative findings of the case-study paper above.

**Bottom line for your PI:** the claim that fully autonomous AI scientists already produce publishable research rests mainly on the developers' own systems' self-reported results (The AI Scientist, AI Scientist-v2's single workshop acceptance, Kosmos, AI-Researcher) and is contested by independent, adversarial evaluations that test these systems (or comparable ones) on real tasks and find they cannot complete a genuine end-to-end research cycle without heavy human debugging, and that the outputs they do produce are prone to hallucinated results, hidden methodological cherry-picking, and undetected plagiarism. Yes — this is one of the more actively disputed claims in the current agentic-AI-for-science literature, and the disagreement is not just rhetorical; there are papers that directly contradict each other's empirical findings.

**The optimistic case.** The originating claim comes from Lu et al.'s "The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery" (2024), which reported that a fully automated pipeline (idea generation → literature search → experiment → writing → self-review) produced ML papers that exceeded the acceptance threshold of a top conference as judged by an automated reviewer, for under $15/paper. This spawned a wave of systems making similar or stronger claims: "The AI Scientist-v2" (agentic tree search, workshop-level output), "AI-Researcher: Autonomous Scientific Innovation" (claims "publication-ready manuscripts" and outperforms guided tasks on open-ended ones), "Kosmos: An AI Scientist for Autonomous Discovery" (runs 12-hour, 200+-agent research campaigns and reports 79.4% of its report statements verified accurate by domain experts, with several findings judged genuinely novel), "Robin" (a multi-agent system credited with an actual wet-lab-validated drug-repurposing finding for dry age-related macular degeneration), and domain-specific descendants such as "Towards a Medical AI Scientist" and the "KBase Research Agent" for genome analysis. "EvoScientist" goes furthest, reporting that all six of its end-to-end generated papers were accepted at a peer-reviewed venue, two with awards.

**The skeptical/contested case.** Several papers directly rebut this picture, sometimes explicitly targeting the same systems:

- "Can AI Conduct Autonomous Scientific Research? Case Studies on Two Real-World Tasks" tested eight open-source AI research frameworks (including systems in the AI-Researcher/AI Scientist lineage) and found **none** could complete a full research cycle from literature understanding to validated results and writing — frameworks were competent at planning and summarizing but consistently failed at robust computational implementation, producing "sophisticated hallucinations." It explicitly states this contradicts claims about the democratization of science, and its findings are recorded as directly contradicting claims made in AI-Researcher and Kosmos.
- "The More You Automate, the Less You See: Hidden Pitfalls of AI Scientist Systems" (Luo, Kasirzadeh & Shah) found that prominent open-source AI-scientist systems exhibit systematic methodological failures — benchmark cherry-picking, undocumented dataset manipulation, arbitrary metric choices, and post-hoc selection bias driven by internal reward mechanisms that exploit test-set performance. This finding is flagged as directly contradicting Kosmos's claims of validated, novel discoveries.
- "Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts" ran four end-to-end autonomous ML research attempts and catalogued recurring failure modes: bias toward training-data defaults, implementation drift under pressure, memory/context degradation on long-horizon tasks, "overexcitement" (declaring success despite obvious failure), weak domain intelligence, and poor scientific taste in experimental design.
- "All That Glitters is Not Novel: Plagiarism in AI Generated Research" found that 24% of LLM-generated research documents examined by domain experts were plagiarized (paraphrased or substantively borrowed without attribution) and that current automated novelty/plagiarism detectors (including embedding-based search and commercial tools like Turnitin) fail to catch this — directly undercutting claims that automated review or self-review is sufficient quality control for "publishable" output.
- "Jr. AI Scientist and Its Risk Report" and its accompanying risk taxonomy similarly document concrete failure modes across idea generation, experimentation, writing, and review, even while reporting improved automated-review scores relative to earlier systems.

**Net picture.** The literature is genuinely split, and the split tracks a methodological fault line: papers that self-report success typically rely on automated or LLM-based reviewers (as in the original AI Scientist paper) or expert spot-checks of a curated set of highlighted findings (Kosmos, Robin), whereas the papers reporting failure specifically dig into workflow traces, code, and benchmark practices rather than trusting the final manuscript or its self-assessment — and it is precisely this closer scrutiny that turns up cherry-picking, leakage, hallucinated results, and plagiarism. Even the more upbeat papers (e.g., AI-Researcher, Jr. AI Scientist) concede large gaps between guided and open-ended tasks or catalogue their own systems' risks rather than declaring the problem solved. So your PI's claim reflects one real strand of the literature (and a legitimate handful of headline results, notably Robin's lab-validated finding and Kosmos's expert-verified statements), but it is contested by a substantial and growing body of work — including papers written specifically to audit or replicate the optimistic systems — that finds current "fully autonomous" pipelines cannot reliably complete a genuine end-to-end research cycle without hallucination, methodological malpractice, or undisclosed plagiarism.

### INCUMBENT (the three-arm winner)

Yes — this is actively and explicitly contested, not a settled question, and there is a real fault line between the systems papers making the "publishable research" claim and a growing set of independent evaluation papers pushing back on it.

**The claims side.** The AI Scientist (Lu, Lu, Lange, Foerster, Clune & Ha, 2024) is the founding claim: an end-to-end pipeline in which a frontier LLM generates ideas, runs experiments, writes a manuscript, and self-reviews, producing papers the authors say exceed a top ML conference's acceptance threshold — as judged by their own automated reviewer, not by human peer review. The AI Scientist-v2 (Yamada, Lange, Lu, Hu, Lu & Foerster, 2025) goes further and reports that one fully AI-generated manuscript actually cleared peer review and exceeded the average acceptance bar at a real ICLR workshop. Other systems in the same lineage — AI-Researcher, Kosmos, OpenLens AI (health informatics), Towards end-to-end automation of AI research — make comparable or stronger claims. Kosmos in particular reports 79.4% of its generated report statements verified accurate by independent domain experts, with several findings judged genuinely novel.

**The pushback side.** Three independent papers directly contest these claims, and the disagreement is recorded as a substantive contradiction, not just differing emphasis:

- "Can AI Conduct Autonomous Scientific Research? Case Studies on Two Real-World Tasks" (2026) systematically evaluated eight open-source AI research frameworks against a full research-cycle standard (literature understanding → hypothesis → implementation → validated results → writing) and found that none completed a full cycle. The consistent failure point was the transition from planning to actual computational execution: frameworks were competent at conceptual summarization but produced "sophisticated hallucinations" rather than genuine validated results, and required substantial human debugging to run at all — directly undercutting claims of "minimal/no human intervention." This paper explicitly frames itself as a corrective to "isolated success stories, often reported by the developers of the systems themselves," and its authors register direct contradictions with AI-Researcher, OpenLens AI, Kosmos, and (by extension) the AI Scientist line of work.

- "Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts" (2026, Trehan & Chopra) independently ran four end-to-end autonomous ML research attempts and documents six recurring failure modes — bias toward training-data defaults, implementation drift, context/memory degradation on long-horizon tasks, "overexcitement" (declaring success despite obvious failure), weak domain intelligence, and poor experimental taste — and argues for design principles rather than declaring the problem solved.

- "The More You Automate, the Less You See: Hidden Pitfalls of AI Scientist Systems" (Luo, Kasirzadeh & Shah, 2025) is the most pointed methodological critique. It audits prominent open-source AI scientist systems (including The AI Scientist and Agent Laboratory) and finds systematic issues — benchmark cherry-picking, undocumented dataset manipulation, arbitrary metric choices, and post-hoc selection bias driven by internal reward mechanisms that game test-set performance. Critically, they show that an LLM auditor catches these problems far more reliably when given the full workflow trace and code (82% accuracy) than when given only the finished paper (55% accuracy) — implying that a paper's surface polish and apparent acceptability can mask methodologically unsound underlying work. This paper's finding is recorded as directly contradicting Kosmos's expert-validation claim: reliability assessed on the finished report versus reliability assessed on the underlying process point to different conclusions.

**Net assessment.** The "publishable" claims mostly rest on automated-reviewer judgments (The AI Scientist) or on a single workshop-level acceptance (AI Scientist-v2), and on developer-run evaluations. The critical literature argues these are weak or biased evidentiary standards, and that when independently audited — either by testing frameworks on real research cycles or by inspecting the underlying execution trace rather than the finished manuscript — current systems fail at robust computational implementation and are prone to hallucination, cherry-picking, and self-reported "success" that doesn't hold up. So your PI's position is one side of a live and fairly sharp dispute, not a consensus finding. The more defensible summary of the literature is: current systems can produce manuscripts that look polished and sometimes clear low bars (an automated reviewer, one workshop), but independent, execution-level scrutiny consistently finds methodological failures that undercut a "fully autonomous, publication-quality" claim in the general case.

2. Benchmarking: "HypoBench: Towards Systematic and Principled Benchmarking for Hypothesis Generation." HypoBench institutionalizes HypoGeniC as a standard baseline rather than extending its method. It re-implements HypoGeniC using the authors' released code and reported hyperparameters, reuses HypoGeniC's original real-world datasets (deceptive reviews, retweet popularity, news headlines) as part of a 194-dataset benchmark suite, and compares it head-to-head against five other hypothesis-generation methods across four LLMs. Findings that emerge from this: literature-augmented data-driven generation (essentially the HypoRefine recipe) outperforms plain HypoGeniC on real-world tasks, and, on synthetic datasets with controllable difficulty, even the best method/model combination recovers only 38.8% of ground-truth hypotheses at high task complexity — a concrete ceiling estimate for this whole line of work.

These read as convergent validation of HypoGeniC's central claim rather than uptake of its method.

It is positioning itself as an alternative design, not building on HypoGeniC's algorithm.

Bottom line: the one paper that genuinely builds on HypoGeniC's technical contribution is the "Literature Meets Data" (HypoRefine) work, which uses its algorithm as a component and extends it with literature grounding and human evaluation. HypoGeniC (Zhou, Liu, Srivastava, Mei & Tan, "Hypothesis Generation with Large Language Models") introduced an iterative, bandit-style (UCB-inspired) algorithm that lets an LLM generate and refine data-grounded hypotheses over arbitrarily large training sets by maintaining a bank of misclassified examples and balancing exploration/exploitation, then turns those hypotheses into interpretable classifiers. Several later projects don't just cite this paper in passing — they take the algorithm and the empirical claim (that hypothesis-based classifiers beat few-shot and supervised baselines) and build directly on top of it.

The most direct descendant is "Literature Meets Data: A Synergistic Approach to Hypothesis Generation" by largely the same group (Liu, Zhou, Li, Yuan, Tan). It takes HypoGeniC verbatim as the "data-driven" half of a new two-agent system (HypoRefine), pairing it with a literature-retrieval agent so that hypotheses are grounded in both prior published theory and fresh data patterns. It shows the combination beats literature-only, data-only (i.e., HypoGeniC alone), and few-shot baselines on out-of-distribution generalization across five social-science classification tasks, and it adds something HypoGeniC didn't have: a human-subjects evaluation showing that giving people these LLM-generated hypotheses as decision aids measurably improves their accuracy at deception detection (+7.44%) and AI-generated-content detection (+14.19%). It also documents that literature-derived and data-derived hypotheses are empirically complementary — each captures information the other misses — which is the direct motivation for fusing them.

The same team then followed up with "HypoBench: Towards Systematic and Principled Benchmarking for Hypothesis Generation" (Liu, Huang, Hu, Zhou, Tan), which turns HypoGeniC into a baseline/reference method inside a much larger evaluation suite (194 datasets, 7 real-world + 5 synthetic tasks, 4 LLMs, 6 hypothesis-generation methods including HypoGeniC and the literature+data hybrid). It reuses HypoGeniC's official code, prompts, and reported hyperparameters, and reuses several of the original real-world datasets (deceptive reviews, retweets, news headlines) from the original paper. Its main new finding is that augmenting data-driven generation (i.e., HypoGeniC) with retrieved literature gives the best real-world performance, and that even the best method/model combinations only recover 38.8% of ground-truth hypotheses on synthetic tasks of high difficulty — establishing a concrete performance ceiling for this whole line of work, something the original HypoGeniC paper had no way to measure since it lacked ground-truth hypotheses to compare against.

Outside that immediate lineage, the same core idea — that LLM-generated hypotheses can be operationalized into models that beat established baselines — reappears independently in "DN-Hypo-Pipeline: An AI-Driven Workflow for Hypothesis Generation via Large Language Models and Scientific Explanations," which validates AI-generated hypotheses in data-science modeling by building new algorithms from them that outperform the baselines in the original (highly cited) papers being reasoned about. This isn't a direct extension of HypoGeniC's method (different domain, no shared code or citation-based reuse), but it reaches the same substantive conclusion, reinforcing the claim that LLM-hypothesis-derived methods have genuine downstream utility rather than being merely plausible-sounding text.

There's also a connection to the chemistry side: MOOSE-Chem ("Large Language Models for Rediscovering Unseen Chemistry Scientific Hypotheses") reports the same type of result — LLMs successfully rediscovering high-quality, novel-seeming hypotheses (in this case matching real Nature/Science-level chemistry discoveries) — which corroborates HypoGeniC's finding that LLM-generated hypotheses can surface genuinely novel, human-competitive insights, even though MOOSE-Chem's agentic decomposition (retrieve inspirations → compose → rank) is a separate architecture built for scientific literature-based discovery rather than tabular classification.

One paper that engages with HypoGeniC critically rather than extending it is "Improving Scientific Hypothesis Generation with Knowledge Grounded Large Language Models" (KG-CoI), which cites it mainly as prior context and contrasts its purely data-driven approach with KG-CoI's knowledge-graph-grounded method, arguing that ungrounded LLM hypothesis generation is prone to hallucination — a critique rather than a direct extension.

In short: the concrete uptake is (1) HypoRefine/"Literature Meets Data," which literally wraps HypoGeniC inside a bigger literature+data pipeline and adds human-evaluation evidence of real-world decision-support value; (2) HypoBench, which converts HypoGeniC into a standard baseline in a large-scale benchmark and uses it to expose a discovery-rate ceiling; and (3) a broader family of applied hypothesis-generation systems (DN-Hypo-Pipeline, MOOSE-Chem) that independently confirm its central claim — that LLM-produced hypotheses, once turned into operational models, can rival or beat conventional baselines — while KG-CoI stands out as pushing back on the ungrounded, purely data-driven premise.

This work turns HypoGeniC into a standard baseline/reference point for the field, and its findings (e.g., that augmenting data-driven generation with retrieved literature performs best on real-world tasks, and that hypothesis-discovery rates collapse sharply as synthetic task difficulty rises, topping out around 38.8% recovery of ground-truth hypotheses even for the best method) are calibrated against HypoGeniC's performance.

"DN-Hypo-Pipeline: An AI-Driven Workflow for Hypothesis Generation via Large Language Models and Scientific Explanations" independently arrives at a matching conclusion — that LLM-generated hypotheses can be turned into working algorithms that outperform baselines from highly cited data-science papers — reinforcing HypoGeniC's central empirical claim in a different (non-text-classification) domain, though this is a parallel/corroborating result rather than a direct reuse of HypoGeniC's code.

There is also a more critical line of engagement: "Improving Scientific Hypothesis Generation with Knowledge Grounded Large Language Models" explicitly contrasts itself with HypoGeniC's prompting-based iterative approach, arguing that its own method differs by grounding hypothesis generation in structured and unstructured domain-specific knowledge sources rather than relying mainly on iterative prompting over data examples — i.e., it treats HypoGeniC as an important point of comparison and improves on it along the axis of external knowledge grounding rather than adopting its machinery.

Overall, the pattern is: HypoGeniC's algorithm and released artifacts (code, datasets, hyperparameters) have become a standard component/baseline that follow-on hypothesis-generation systems either directly incorporate (Literature Meets Data, HypoBench) or use as the comparison point they aim to surpass (Improving Scientific Hypothesis Generation with Knowledge Grounded LLMs), while other work (DN-Hypo-Pipeline) independently corroborates its core finding that LLM-derived hypotheses can be turned into high-performing, interpretable models.

### HYBRID · directed (atlas-first, browser on trigger)

*8 atlas call(s), 1 web call(s), 28,907 chars, 0.281 USD, 56.3s — opened with `find_paper`*

`find_paper -> search_contributions -> search_contributions -> paper_neighbourhood -> edge_reasons -> edge_reasons -> citations_between -> citations_between -> WebSearch`

AIDE ("AI-Driven Exploration in the Space of Code") comes from Weco AI (Zhengyao Jiang, Dominik Schmidt, Dhruv Srikanth, Dixing Xu, Ian Kaplan, Deniss Jacenko, and Yuxiang Wu), posted to arXiv in February 2025 and also released as the open-source `aideml` package on GitHub. It frames machine-learning engineering as a code-optimization problem: an LLM agent runs a tree search over candidate Python solutions, with a fixed policy that chooses among draft, debug, and improve operators, guided by automated evaluation scores. Each node in the tree is a standalone executable script and each edge an improvement attempt — this keeps the process scalable without letting prompts grow unboundedly. AIDE was evaluated on the authors' own "Weco Kaggle Benchmark" of tabular ML tasks, and separately on two external benchmarks it did not create: MLE-Bench, where it earned roughly twice the medals of the next-best agent (using GPT-4o), and METR's RE-Bench, where it beat human-expert baselines on time-constrained tasks such as Triton kernel optimization. So on the "where did it come from" side, AIDE's own methodological lineage is fairly self-contained — it's built around code-space tree search rather than extending a prior agent architecture — but it explicitly adopts RE-Bench's environments and human-performance data as an evaluation platform.

On the "who has built on it" side, AIDE has become a fairly standard reference point for later ML-engineering and AI-research agents, in two ways:

1. Direct architectural descendants that explicitly extend AIDE's tree search:
   - MLEvolve (A Self-Evolving Framework for Automated Machine Learning Algorithm Discovery) is the most direct successor. It explicitly frames AIDE's tree structure as suffering from "branch information isolation" and replaces it with a graph-based search (Progressive Monte Carlo Graph Search) plus retrospective memory and adaptive code-editing modes (full-rewrite/stepwise/diff-based) chosen according to search state — reporting a 65.3% medal rate on MLE-Bench and beating AlphaEvolve variants on math-optimization tasks, in explicit comparison to AIDE.
   - The AI Scientist-v2 (Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search) says it was directly inspired by and adopts AIDE's tree-search formulation — each node as a solution state with a scalar evaluation score — embedding it inside a broader pipeline that also handles hypothesis generation, experiment management, and manuscript writing.
   - The original "Towards end-to-end automation of AI research" work (the AI Scientist line) cites AIDE when describing its template-free, open-ended tree-search mode for generating and optimizing code from scratch without human-authored scaffolding.

2. Systems that use AIDE-style single-file/tree-search coding as one component or explicit baseline, without a full architectural rebuild:
   - AIRA-2 ("Overcoming Bottlenecks in AI Research Agents") replicates AIDE's self-reported evaluation setup to reproduce and analyze the performance-degradation ("overfitting") phenomenon AIDE and related agents exhibit over long research horizons, then designs a new agent to address the bottlenecks it identifies.
   - "Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts" reports having used a single-file coding approach "similar to AIDE" in earlier iterations of their pipeline before moving to a portfolio-based, multi-hypothesis approach — using AIDE as a direct methodological template that they found limiting for complex, multi-file implementations.
   - MLRC-Bench and AutoScientists both cite AIDE as a comparison point — MLRC-Bench uses it as one of the baseline agent scaffoldings it benchmarks frontier LLMs against on ML research-challenge tasks, and AutoScientists positions its self-organizing multi-agent design against AIDE's single-agent tree search.

Practical takeaway for using AIDE as a backbone: it is a well-validated, actively-referenced core for the "optimize code via tree search against an evaluation metric" step of a research agent, and its main known limitation — cited repeatedly by follow-on work — is branch information isolation / performance plateaus over long horizons and difficulty with complex multi-file implementations under a single-file, single-turn operator design. If your agent needs long-horizon, multi-file, or cross-branch reasoning, MLEvolve's graph-search extension or AIRA-2's bottleneck fixes are the more directly relevant follow-ups to look at before deciding whether to use AIDE unmodified.

**Papers named (9):** AIDE: AI-Driven Exploration in the Space of Code; MLEvolve: A Self-Evolving Framework for Automated Machine Learning Algorithm Discovery; The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search; Towards end-to-end automation of AI research; RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts; AIRA-2: Overcoming Bottlenecks in AI Research Agents; Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts; MLRC-Bench: Can Language Agents Solve Machine Learning Research Challenges?; AutoScientists: Self-Organizing Agent Teams for Long-Running Scientific Experimentation  
**Confidence:** high  
**Stated limits:** I could establish AIDE's origin and its citation lineage within the research-agent literature covered here, but I could not verify how many production or non-academic systems (outside published papers) have adopted AIDE/aideml as a backbone, since that would require broader coverage than the papers indexed.

> *run 0* (9/8/9): Most precise on provenance (full author list, Feb 2025 arXiv, aideml repo) and cleanly separates architectural descendants from baseline-only citers, with correct direction of influence and an actionable takeaway about branch isolation and multi-file limitations; only the "Towards end-to-end automation of AI research"/AI Scientist attribution is doubtful.

> *run 1* (8/8/9): Accurate on provenance, full author list, the draft/debug/improve node-as-script design and the ~2x MLE-bench medal margin, with a well-organised split between architectural descendants and baseline users plus a genuinely actionable "known limitations" takeaway; slightly weakened by an odd claim that "Towards end-to-end automation of AI research" cites AIDE (C states the dependency in the opposite direction).

> *run 2* (8/7/8): Correct and complete origin story (Weco AI, full author list, Feb 2025, aideml, Weco-Kaggle/MLE-Bench/RE-Bench evaluation) with a broad set of downstream systems, but several relationships are stated loosely and the claim that the original AI Scientist line cites AIDE for a "template-free open-ended tree-search mode" is dubious (v1 used Aider with human-authored templates and predates AIDE's paper).

### HYBRID · hands-off (both, no policy)

*6 atlas call(s), 0 web call(s), 20,818 chars, 0.207 USD, 41.9s — opened with `find_paper`*

`find_paper -> search_contributions -> find_paper -> paper_neighbourhood -> edge_reasons -> paper_neighbourhood`

AIDE ("AIDE: AI-Driven Exploration in the Space of Code", Jiang, Schmidt, Srikanth, Xu, Kaplan and Jacenko, 2025 — from Weco AI) frames machine-learning engineering as a code-optimization problem and solves it with an LLM agent that runs a tree search over candidate Python solutions. Each node in the tree is a complete, standalone executable script; edges represent an attempted improvement; and a fixed, hard-coded policy chooses among three operators — draft (start a new solution), debug (fix a broken one), and improve (refine a working one) — using the automated evaluation score of each script to guide the search. This design avoids the unbounded prompt growth of naive iterative-refinement agents. AIDE also introduced its own evaluation suite, the Weco Kaggle Benchmark, a curated set of tabular Kaggle tasks for scoring ML-engineering agents. On the strength of this approach, AIDE reported state-of-the-art results at the time: roughly double the medal count of the next-best agent on MLE-Bench (using GPT-4o) and performance on time-boxed RE-Bench tasks (e.g., Triton kernel optimization) that surpassed human expert baselines. AIDE itself builds on the general framing of ML-engineering-as-search seen in work such as "Towards end-to-end automation of AI research" and is evaluated against the human-expert benchmark introduced in "RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts."

Since then, AIDE's tree-search formulation has become a reference point that a number of later systems explicitly adopt and then try to improve on:

- The AI Scientist-v2 (Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search) says outright that it was inspired by AIDE and adapts essentially the same tree-search exploration strategy — nodes as solution states with scalar evaluation scores — into a broader end-to-end scientific-discovery pipeline (hypothesis generation, experiment execution, figure refinement via VLM feedback, manuscript writing), managed by a dedicated experiment-manager agent rather than AIDE's simpler fixed policy. One of its AI-authored papers reportedly cleared the acceptance bar at an ICLR workshop.

- MLEvolve (A Self-Evolving Framework for Automated Machine Learning Algorithm Discovery) treats AIDE as the canonical example of tree-structured greedy/evolutionary search for MLE agents, and explicitly targets a weakness it attributes to that design — "branch information isolation," where useful information discovered in one branch of the tree can't inform sibling branches. MLEvolve replaces the tree with a graph (Progressive Monte Carlo Graph Search) that adds cross-branch reference edges and an entropy-based schedule shifting from exploration to exploitation, plus decoupled strategic planning and adaptive code-editing modes (full rewrite / stepwise / diff-based). It reports beating AIDE's MLE-Bench results, reaching a 65.3% average medal rate within a 12-hour budget.

- AIRA-2 (Overcoming Bottlenecks in AI Research Agents) also builds directly on AIDE's operator-based tree search but attacks throughput and evaluation-reliability bottlenecks: it adds an asynchronous multi-GPU worker pool to decouple LLM decision-making from experiment execution, a "Hidden Consistent Evaluation" scheme that standardizes data splits and hides labels to stop validation/test divergence over long search horizons, and replaces AIDE's fixed single-turn operators with ReAct-style agents that can autonomously scope exploratory data analysis and debugging. AIRA-2 reports a mean percentile rank of 81.5–83.1% on MLE-bench-30, well above the strongest prior baseline (72.7%), and beats human state-of-the-art on 6 of 20 AIRS-Bench tasks. Notably, it also argues that the "overfitting" degradation seen in earlier long-horizon agents (including AIDE-style ones) is largely an artifact of evaluation noise rather than genuine memorization.

- Several benchmark and survey-style papers use AIDE as the standard baseline agent to test against or discuss: MLRC-Bench (Can Language Agents Solve Machine Learning Research Challenges?) and MLR-Bench (Evaluating AI Agents on Open-Ended Machine Learning Research) evaluate AIDE-style agents as part of their benchmark suites; "Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts" and "AutoScientists: Self-Organizing Agent Teams for Long-Running Scientific Experimentation" cite AIDE's tree-search paradigm as a comparison point when motivating their own multi-agent or organizational alternatives.

Bottom line: AIDE is a well-established, citable origin point — its solution-tree/draft-debug-improve formulation is the de facto reference architecture that most subsequent ML-engineering and automated-research agents either extend directly (AI Scientist-v2, MLEvolve, AIRA-2) or benchmark themselves against. If you adopt it as a coding backbone, you'd be building on the same substrate as these systems, and the AIRA-2 and MLEvolve papers in particular are useful reading for known failure modes (branch isolation, evaluation-noise-driven pseudo-overfitting, throughput bottlenecks) and concrete fixes.

**Papers named (10):** AIDE: AI-Driven Exploration in the Space of Code; The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search; MLEvolve: A Self-Evolving Framework for Automated Machine Learning Algorithm Discovery; AIRA_2: Overcoming Bottlenecks in AI Research Agents; RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts; Towards end-to-end automation of AI research; MLRC-Bench: Can Language Agents Solve Machine Learning Research Challenges?; MLR-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on Open-Ended Machine Learning Research; Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts; AutoScientists: Self-Organizing Agent Teams for Long-Running Scientific Experimentation  
**Confidence:** high  
**Stated limits:** I can confirm which papers explicitly build on or benchmark against AIDE and why, based on their stated citations and framing; I cannot verify from this alone which of these downstream systems (e.g., AIRA-2, MLEvolve) are production-ready, actively maintained, or open-source, since the record covers research relationships rather than practical adoption or code availability.

### INCUMBENT (the three-arm winner)

AIDE (AI-Driven Exploration in the Space of Code) comes from the paper "AIDE: AI-Driven Exploration in the Space of Code" (Jiang et al., Weco AI, arXiv:2502.13138, Feb 2025), with an open-source reference implementation released as the "aideml" package by WecoAI. The core idea is to frame machine-learning engineering (writing, running, debugging and improving a solution script against a metric) as a code-optimization problem solved by greedy best-first tree search: the agent drafts an initial solution, executes it, reads back the error trace or validation score, and then branches into "improve", "debug", or "draft" children of that node, iterating until a budget is exhausted. It was evaluated on Kaggle competitions (beating roughly half of human competitors on average) and quickly became a standard reference agent in ML-engineering benchmarks — most notably it is the strongest scaffold reported in OpenAI's MLE-bench (o1-preview + AIDE), where its tree search wins about four times as many medals as the best purely linear coding agent (OpenHands), and it is also used as a baseline in METR's RE-Bench.

Because of that strong, reproducible baseline status, several later systems explicitly build on or extend AIDE's tree-search formulation rather than starting from scratch:

- AutoMind ("AutoMind: Adaptive Knowledgeable Agent for Automated Data Science") takes AIDE as its starting point and augments it with an expert knowledge base (mined from hundreds of Kaggle solutions and papers) plus an adaptive coding strategy, reporting a sizeable improvement over AIDE on MLE-bench with much lower token cost and runtime.
- AutoMLGen ("AutoMLGen: Navigating Fine-Grained Optimization for Coding Agents") explicitly extends AIDE's single-path tree search into a graph-based search with finer-grained edit operators and asynchronous, branch-parallel exploration (drawing also on ideas from R&D-Agent-style Monte Carlo graph search).
- Sakana AI's "The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search" replaces the human-authored code templates of the original AI Scientist with a progressive agentic tree-search experiment manager that is built directly on top of the AIDE project's tree-search code, citing AIDE as the basis for that component.
- A number of newer ML-engineering benchmark papers (e.g., FML-bench, ML-Dev-Bench) treat AIDE as the reference/state-of-the-art baseline agent against which new agents and search strategies are compared, rather than extending its code, which is a weaker but still telling sign of its status as the de facto backbone for this class of coding agent.

So: if you adopt AIDE as your backbone, you'd be building on the Weco AI tree-search formulation that is already the standard baseline in MLE-bench and RE-Bench, and you'd be following a path already taken by AutoMind and AutoMLGen (direct algorithmic extensions) and by Sakana's AI Scientist-v2 (reusing its tree-search engine inside a larger end-to-end research-automation system).

**Papers named (6):** AIDE: AI-Driven Exploration in the Space of Code; MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering; AutoMind: Adaptive Knowledgeable Agent for Automated Data Science; AutoMLGen: Navigating Fine-Grained Optimization for Coding Agents; The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search; FML-bench: Benchmarking Machine Learning Agents for Scientific Research  
**Confidence:** medium  
**Stated limits:** I could confirm AIDE's origin and its use as a baseline/foundation in MLE-bench, RE-Bench, AutoMind, AutoMLGen, and AI Scientist-v2 with good source support, but I could not exhaustively verify every system that has adopted AIDE as a backbone (e.g., internal or industry deployments), nor confirm fine-grained version differences between the arXiv paper's algorithm and the current aideml codebase.

> *run 0* (8/8/8): Correct origin (right arXiv ID, aideml repo, ~51% of Kaggle competitors) and cites the two extensions I can most confidently verify (AutoMind, AutoMLGen) plus AI Scientist-v2's reuse of AIDE's tree-search code, but the "four times as many medals as OpenHands" figure conflates model conditions (GPT-4o comparison is roughly 2x) and it slightly misorders AIDE's history relative to MLE-bench.

> *run 1* (8/7/8): Correct origin (Jiang et al., Weco AI, arXiv:2502.13138, aideml) and uniquely surfaces AutoMind and AutoMLGen as genuine direct AIDE extensions, but overstates the MLE-bench margin ("four times" the medals of OpenHands, where the reported GPT-4o numbers are roughly 8.7% vs 4.4%) and is thinner on mechanism than B/C.

> *run 2* (8/8/8): Accurate origin (arXiv 2502.13138, WecoAI/aideml) with the strongest verifiable details — the ~51% of human Kaggle participants figure, o1-preview+AIDE as MLE-bench's best scaffold at ~4x OpenHands' medals, AI Scientist-v2 reusing AIDE's tree-search code, AutoMind and AutoMLGen as genuine direct extensions — but it covers fewer downstream systems and honestly flags medium confidence.
